summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to understand why estimating variance of K-fold cross-validation is difficult, given that cross-validation is widely used to assess generalization error and compare algorithms but its variance can be very large, motivating a theoretical analysis of whether any estimator of this variance can be unbiased across all data distributions.

A researcher wants the general performance measure framework distinguishing application-oriented evaluation, which cares about the best algorithm for one specific training set, from algorithm-oriented evaluation, which cares about the sensitivity of a learning algorithm to the choice of training examples across many possible training sets.

A researcher wants the formal definitions of prediction error and expected prediction error, the two measures of a learning algorithm's accuracy, one conditional on a specific training set and the other averaged over training sets drawn from the underlying distribution, together with the observation that estimating the uncertainty of these measures is often overlooked.
summaries.primary_concept: prediction error and expected prediction error
sub_concepts: prediction error and expected prediction error

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know why a hold-out variance estimator that ignores correlations between test errors is badly biased even with several independent training and test sets available, contrasted with an alternative estimator that accounts for these correlations and remains unbiased, illustrated through a simple linear regression simulation.

A researcher wants the formal definition of the K-fold cross-validation estimator as an average of test errors across disjoint blocks, together with the debate over whether it should be interpreted as an unbiased estimate of the prediction error of a specific training set or of the expected prediction error at a slightly reduced training sample size.

A researcher wants the cross-validation with matched pairs estimator used to compare two algorithms on the same train-test splits, avoiding the extra variability that would come from independent cross-validation runs, together with the related jackknife and delete-m jackknife estimators used to estimate the optimism bias of the training error.

A researcher wants the covariance matrix block structure of cross-validation errors, derived from symmetry arguments over permutations of examples, showing that the covariance matrix has only three distinct values corresponding to a variance term, a within-block covariance, and a between-blocks covariance, together with the resulting three-component decomposition of the total variance.

A researcher wants the no unbiased estimator theorem for the variance of K-fold cross-validation, proved first by showing that only quadratic-form estimators can be unbiased and then by showing that no linear combination of the three quadratic invariants can match the true three-component variance for every possible distribution of the errors.
summaries.answer_type: main negative result with proof sketch

summaries.information_need: A researcher wants the eigenanalysis of the covariance matrix of cross-validation errors, showing that it has exactly three eigenvalues with multiplicities tied to the number of examples and the number of folds, together with the insight that the component corresponding to the overall mean has only one effective realization, which explains why its variance cannot be estimated without bias.

A researcher wants the bounds on the variance components within-block and between-blocks covariance derived from Cauchy-Schwarz and non-negativity constraints on the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix, together with the observation that the admissible region for these two components is wide enough that no universally small-bias variance estimate can be constructed.

An analyst wants an empirical decomposition of cross-validation variance into its three orthogonal components for a simulated regression problem with and without outliers, finding that the between-blocks component dominates at small sample sizes and stays comparable to the variance term at larger sample sizes when outliers are present, and that the number of folds affects the balance among components without a universally optimal choice.

An analyst wants an empirical variance decomposition on real classification data for a tree-based classifier evaluated by K-fold cross-validation, finding that the variance term alone accounts for only a modest majority of the total variance, so that a variance estimate based on it alone would carry a substantial negative bias.
summaries.primary_concept: empirical variance decomposition on real classification data
sub_concepts: empirical variance decomposition on real classification data

summaries.field: machine learning / model evaluation special cases
summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know how the hold-out special case of the general variance result works, since independence between training and test sets forces the between-blocks covariance to vanish, removing one of the three unsatisfiable constraints and allowing an unbiased variance estimate when several independent training and test sets are available.

summaries.field: machine learning / model evaluation special cases
summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know why the two-fold cross-validation special case still exhibits a nonzero between-blocks covariance despite its non-overlapping training blocks, arising from the fact that each training block coincides exactly with the other fold's test block, which prevents the general negative result from being circumvented in this case.

summaries.field: machine learning / model evaluation special cases
summaries.information_need: A researcher wants to know why the leave-one-out cross-validation special case, in which each fold contains a single held-out example, still admits no unbiased variance estimator despite its simplified covariance structure without within-block terms, since the same unsatisfiable linear constraints on the estimator coefficients persist in this limiting case.
